::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a receptionist and a reference number"}
A company's receptionist reads incoming letters' return addresses and decides which replies to hand back to which couriers. A courier from an unknown company still gets their letter delivered and processed; they just aren't handed the reply. And when you send the same order twice by mistake, with the same reference number, a good supplier notices and doesn't ship twice.

**CORS** is that receptionist for browsers. An **idempotency key** is that reference number.
:::

## The problem

Two situations every web API meets sooner or later.

**A page on another website calls the API.** Atlas's own web UI lives at the same address as the API. But someone will build a front end hosted elsewhere, and some other page, maybe a hostile one, will try to call Atlas from a visitor's browser. Here's a page served from `http://localhost:9000`, a different **origin** from Atlas's `http://localhost:8000`, run in a real browser (Chromium, driven by Playwright):

```html
<pre id="out">running</pre>
<script>
  // A page on a different origin tries to read Atlas's public issues list.
  fetch("http://localhost:8000/issues?limit=1")
    .then((response) => response.json())
    .then((body) => { document.getElementById("out").textContent = "read: " + body.items[0].title; })
    .catch((error) => { document.getElementById("out").textContent = "failed: " + error; });
</script>
```
```text
http://localhost:9000/other-site.html -> failed: TypeError: Failed to fetch
  console: Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/issues?limit=1' from origin 'http://localhost:9000' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
```

The browser refused to let the page read the answer. But look at Atlas's log at that moment:

```text
{"time": "2026-11-19T09:13:36.241494+00:00", "level": "INFO", "logger": "atlas.api", "message": "request finished", "request_id": "ae7adfa1ef0f4b3ea7762995239f01db", "method": "GET", "path": "/issues", "status": 200, "duration_ms": 55.8}
```

The request *arrived and was answered*, 200. The browser only hid the response from the page. Whether that's protection or not depends on what the request did, which is the point of this lesson.

**A POST whose answer never arrives.** An admin's client sends "add repository `sktime/sktime`", and the connection drops before the response comes back. Did it work? The client can't know, so it sends the request again:

```text
without a key:
  first -> 201 {"id":7,"full_name":"sktime/sktime","indexed_at":null}
  retry -> 409 {"error":{"code":"repo_already_tracked","message":"sktime/sktime is already tracked","request_id":"6d3f15c6fbbb48eea5ce7bcd81a24c3d"}}
```

The retry says "already tracked". Was that the client's own first request, or did someone else add it a moment earlier? The client can't tell success from conflict. For resources without a unique name, like lesson 4.20's notes, the retry would quietly create a duplicate instead.

## Theory

### Origins and the same-origin policy

An **origin** is a scheme, host and port together: `http://localhost:8000` and `http://localhost:9000` are different origins, and so are `http://` and `https://` versions of the same site. Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: a page may *send* requests to other origins, but may not *read* their responses unless the other origin allows it. Without this rule, any website you visit could read your webmail or your bank account through your logged-in browser.

### CORS

**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server tells browsers which other origins may read its responses: it adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers to its answers. For requests that could change things or carry custom headers (like `Authorization`), the browser first sends a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request asking "may this origin send a POST with these headers?". Only if the server says yes does the real request go out.

What CORS is and isn't:

- It's enforced **by browsers**, on behalf of their users. curl, scripts and servers ignore it completely.
- It controls **reading responses**, and for non-simple requests, sending them at all. Simple `GET`s are still sent and still run on the server, as the log above showed.
- It is **not authentication**. Atlas's real protection is that its private routes need a bearer token, and a page on another origin can't get the token: it's kept in `sessionStorage`, which browsers also separate by origin (lesson 4.8).

### Idempotency keys

A request is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once (lesson 4.3). `PUT` and `DELETE` are; `POST` isn't. An **idempotency key** makes a `POST` safe to retry: the client generates a unique `Idempotency-Key` header and sends the same key with each retry of the same operation. The server stores the response under the key the first time, and replays it for repeats instead of doing the work again. Stripe's API popularised the pattern; an IETF draft standardises the header.

Two rules make it work:

- The stored response is saved **in the same transaction** as the change it describes, so there's no moment where one exists without the other.
- Keys are **scoped to the user**. Clients choose them, so they can collide (two clients using `"1"`) or be guessed. A key from one user must never reach another user's stored response.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Atlas
  participant DB as Postgres
  C->>A: POST /repos (Idempotency-Key: k1)
  A->>DB: key k1 for this user? no
  A->>DB: insert repo + store response under (user, k1), one transaction
  A--xC: response lost
  C->>A: POST /repos (Idempotency-Key: k1), retry
  A->>DB: key k1 for this user? yes
  A-->>C: the stored 201 response, replayed
```

### Conventions Atlas follows

Plural resource nouns; JSON everywhere with `snake_case` fields; times in UTC, ISO 8601 (`2026-11-18T03:10:48Z`); 201 and the created resource for POST; 204 for empty successes; `limit` with a maximum on every list; errors in one shape with stable codes (lesson 4.14); an `Idempotency-Key` accepted on every POST that creates something; versioning by adding fields, never changing their meaning (a `/v2/` prefix only if a breaking change is ever unavoidable).

## In the project

### CORS

In `create_app`:

```python
    # Added after request_id, so it wraps it: CORS headers are on every response, errors included.
    app.add_middleware(
        CORSMiddleware,
        allow_origins=settings.cors_origins,
        allow_methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
        allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type", "Idempotency-Key", "X-Request-ID"],
    )
```

`settings.cors_origins` (lesson 4.2) defaults to Atlas's own origin. The test, written first:

```python
def test_cors_allows_only_configured_origins(client: TestClient) -> None:
    preflight = {"Access-Control-Request-Method": "GET"}

    allowed = client.options("/repos", headers={"Origin": "http://localhost:8000", **preflight})
    blocked = client.options("/repos", headers={"Origin": "https://evil.example", **preflight})

    assert allowed.headers["access-control-allow-origin"] == "http://localhost:8000"
    assert "access-control-allow-origin" not in blocked.headers
```

The preflight, by hand:

```text
$ curl -s -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8000/repos -H "Origin: http://localhost:8000" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...
access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Accept, Accept-Language, Authorization, Content-Language, Content-Type, Idempotency-Key, X-Request-ID
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:8000

$ curl -s -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8000/repos -H "Origin: https://evil.example" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST"
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
...
Disallowed CORS origin
```

Allowing a front end hosted elsewhere is configuration, not code. The same browser test, with Atlas started with `CORS_ORIGINS='["http://localhost:8000", "http://localhost:9001"]'`:

```text
http://localhost:9000/other-site.html -> failed: TypeError: Failed to fetch
  console: Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/issues?limit=1' from origin 'http://localhost:9000' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
http://localhost:9001/other-site.html -> read: Support new metric
```

And from outside any browser, nothing changes:

```text
$ curl -s "http://localhost:8000/issues?limit=1"
{"items":[{"id":1,"repo":"pytorch/ignite","number":20,"title":"Support new metric","url":"...
```

### Red: what retrying must guarantee

Two tests in `tests/test_api_resources.py`: retries replay, and keys belong to one user.

```python
def test_idempotency_key_replays_instead_of_repeating(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    admin = admin_headers(client, session)
    headers = {**admin, "Idempotency-Key": "add-ignite-1"}

    first = client.post("/repos", json={"full_name": "pytorch/ignite"}, headers=headers)
    retry = client.post("/repos", json={"full_name": "pytorch/ignite"}, headers=headers)

    assert first.status_code == retry.status_code == 201
    assert retry.json() == first.json()


def test_idempotency_keys_belong_to_one_user(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    """Keys are chosen by clients and can collide or be guessed (lesson 4.16)."""
    ada = {**admin_headers(client, session), "Idempotency-Key": "add-1"}
    grace = sign_up(client, "grace@example.com")
    session.execute(update(User).where(User.email == "grace@example.com").values(role="admin"))
    session.commit()
    grace = {**grace, "Idempotency-Key": "add-1"}

    client.post("/repos", json={"full_name": "pytorch/ignite"}, headers=ada)
    graces = client.post("/repos", json={"full_name": "sktime/sktime"}, headers=grace)

    assert graces.status_code == 201
    assert graces.json()["full_name"] == "sktime/sktime"
```

Two admins happen to choose the same key, `add-1`, for different operations.

### Green: `api/idempotency.py`

The keys live in a table, `idempotency_keys`, unique per `(user_id, key)`:

```python
def replay(session: Session, user: User, key: str | None, path: str) -> JSONResponse | None:
    """The stored response for this key, or None if the request is new."""
    if key is None:
        return None
    stored = session.scalar(
        select(IdempotencyKey).where(IdempotencyKey.user_id == user.id, IdempotencyKey.key == key)
    )
    if stored is None:
        return None

    used_for_another_request = stored.request_path != path
    if used_for_another_request:
        raise ApiError(
            status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT,
            "idempotency_key_reused",
            "This Idempotency-Key was already used for a different request",
        )
    return JSONResponse(stored.response_body, status_code=stored.response_status)


def remember(
    session: Session, user: User, key: str | None, path: str, status_code: int, body: Any
) -> None:
    """Store the response in the same transaction as the change it describes."""
    if key is None:
        return
    session.add(IdempotencyKey(user_id=user.id, key=key, request_path=path,
                               response_status=status_code, response_body=body))
```

`POST /repos` uses both, around its work:

```python
    previous = idempotency.replay(session, admin, idempotency_key, request.url.path)
    if previous is not None:
        return previous
    ...
    session.add(repo)
    session.flush()
    payload = RepoOut.model_validate(repo).model_dump(mode="json")
    idempotency.remember(
        session, admin, idempotency_key, request.url.path, status.HTTP_201_CREATED, payload
    )
    session.commit()
```

`idempotency_key: Annotated[str | None, Header(max_length=100)] = None` in the route's parameters reads the `Idempotency-Key` header (FastAPI converts underscores to hyphens). `session.flush()` sends the insert so the new row has its `id`, without committing; the single `commit()` then saves the repository and the stored response together.

The lost-response scenario again, with a key:

```text
with Idempotency-Key: add-sktime-7f3a:
  first -> 201 {"id":8,"full_name":"sktime/sktime","indexed_at":null}
  retry -> 201 {"id":8,"full_name":"sktime/sktime","indexed_at":null}
```

The retry gets the same answer as the first attempt, so the client knows its operation happened exactly once.

## Attack it: a borrowed key

What if `replay` looked keys up by key alone, forgetting the user? The second test, against that version:

```text
E       AssertionError: assert 'pytorch/ignite' == 'sktime/sktime'
```

Grace asked to add `sktime/sktime`, and got back Ada's stored response for `pytorch/ignite`, with status 201. Her repository was never added, and she was told it had been. When the stored response holds private data (a note's text, in lesson 4.20), the same bug hands one user another user's data, by guessing a key as simple as `"1"`. Filtering by `user_id` closes it, and the test proves it stays closed.

## Trade-offs: cookies, CSRF and keys *(deep dive)*

**Why the CORS story would be different with cookies.** Atlas sends its token in an `Authorization` header, which a page on another origin can't add for you. If Atlas used a **session cookie** instead, the browser would attach it automatically to *any* request to Atlas, including one sent by a hostile page. CORS would stop that page reading the answer, but, as the log showed, the request would still run. A hostile page could make a logged-in user's browser `POST /repos` or delete a note. That's **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery), and cookie-based APIs defend against it with `SameSite` cookies and CSRF tokens (lesson 7.10).

| Approach | CORS's role | CSRF risk | Token theft risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bearer token in `sessionStorage` (Atlas) | controls which pages may read responses | none from other sites: they can't attach the token | a script running on Atlas's own page could read it |
| Session cookie, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` | same | mostly blocked by `SameSite`; add CSRF tokens for safety | scripts can't read it |

**Where idempotency keys live.** Atlas stores them in Postgres, in the same transaction as the work: simple and exactly right for one database. Larger systems often keep them in a fast store like Redis (Part 5) with an expiry, which is quicker but loses the "same transaction" guarantee, so the design then has to handle a crash between the work and the key. Keys also shouldn't live forever: this lesson's stretch adds an expiry.

## Common mistakes

- **`allow_origins=["*"]`** "to make the error go away". It allows every site, and browsers refuse it outright for requests that carry credentials. List the origins you mean.
- **Thinking CORS protects the API.** It restrains browsers on behalf of their users. Authentication protects the API.
- **Assuming a blocked request didn't run.** Simple requests run; only the response is hidden.
- **Storing idempotency keys in a separate transaction** from the change: a crash in between breaks the guarantee.
- **Idempotency keys shared across users**: one user can be replayed another's response.
- **Retrying POSTs without a key**: duplicates, or a 409 the client can't interpret.

## Check yourself

**1.** The blocked page in "The problem" got `Failed to fetch`. Did Atlas do the work? How do you know?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: Atlas's log has a "request finished" line for `/issues` with status 200 at that moment. A simple GET isn't preflighted, so the browser sent it; CORS only stopped the page from reading the response.
:::

**2.** Why doesn't Atlas's bearer token need CSRF protection, when a session cookie would?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Browsers attach cookies automatically to every request to their site, even requests started by other sites' pages. A bearer token has to be added to each request by Atlas's own JavaScript, and other origins can't read Atlas's `sessionStorage`, so a hostile page has no way to attach it.
:::

**3.** Why must the idempotency record be saved in the same transaction as the new repository?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If they were separate, a crash after creating the repository but before storing the key would let a retry try to create it again, and get the very 409 the key was meant to prevent. One transaction makes them all-or-nothing.
:::

## Exercise

Send the same `Idempotency-Key` to two *different* paths: `POST /repos`, then, once lesson 4.20's notes exist, `POST /issues/{id}/notes`. What happens, and why is that the right answer?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The second request gets 422 with code `idempotency_key_reused`. Replaying the first response would answer a different request with the wrong result; doing the work would break the promise that a key names "this one operation". The reference test `test_note_creation_honours_idempotency_keys` checks this.
:::

## Stretch

Idempotency keys are kept forever. Make `replay` ignore keys older than 24 hours, test first: make a request with a key, age its row with `update(IdempotencyKey).values(created_at=...)` through the test session, and repeat the request.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In `replay`, add `IdempotencyKey.created_at > datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(hours=24)` to the `where`. In the test, after ageing the row, the repeated `POST /repos` does the work again and, since the repository exists, gets 409 `repo_already_tracked`. A real system would also delete old keys on a schedule (Part 5). Not in the reference code.
:::
